Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM2318 : Biosensor and Biotransducers { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fundamentals of Instrumentation and Transducers
Introduction to electrical quantities and units. Functional elements of instrumentation systems. Static and dynamic characteristics: Accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, drift, and hysteresis. Analog and digital measurement principles: CRO, energy meters, time and frequency meters, and multimeters. Classification of transducers: Resistive strain gauges, RTD, LVDT, piezoelectric, electromagnetic, and optical transducers. Applications of transducers in biomedical science.
Module 2: Generalized Instrumentation and Measurement Techniques
General properties and design criteria for input transducers. Static characteristics: Linearity, reproducibility, input/output impedance. Dynamic characteristics: First-order and second-order systems, transfer functions, time delay, error-free instruments. Measurement of displacement, motion, and pressure: Resistive elements: Potentiometers, strain gauges, and bridge circuits. Inductive elements: Variable inductance and LVDT. Capacitive and piezoelectric elements. Types of diaphragms, bellows, and Bourdon tubes. Temperature measurement: Thermistors, thermocouples, RTDs, IC-based sensors, and radiation sensors.
Module 3: Biopotential Electrodes and Interfaces
Electrodes-electrolyte interface: Half-cell potential, polarization, and electrode impedance. Polarizable and non-polarizable electrodes. Electrode circuit models and motion artifacts. Body surface electrodes, internal electrodes (needle and wire types), and microelectrodes (metal and micropipette-based). Applications in ECG, EEG, and EMG monitoring.
Module 4: Chemical Sensors and Biosensors
Blood gas and acid-base physiology sensors: pH, pO2, pCO2 electrodes. Potentiometric and amperometric sensors. Ion-selective electrodes, ISFETs, and Clark electrodes. Fiber optic sensors: Principles and applications in temperature, chemical, and pressure sensing. Biosensor classifications: Biological and transduction phenomena. Enzyme-based and electrode-based sensors, catalytic biosensors, and immunosensors.
Module 5: Advanced Biosensor Technologies and Applications
Design and fabrication of fiber optic sensors. Integration of biosensors in clinical and industrial applications. Non-invasive biosensors for blood-gas and glucose monitoring. Applications of biosensors in the bioprocess industry and environmental analysis. Introduction to biochips and their applications in genomics and diagnostics. Case studies on advanced biosensors and emerging trends.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide a comprehensive understanding of instrumentation systems, transducers, and their static and dynamic characteristics for biomedical and industrial applications.
2 .

To explore the principles and applications of biopotential electrodes, chemical sensors, and biosensors, with a focus on their role in biomedical monitoring and diagnostics.
3 .

To develop an in-depth understanding of measurement techniques for displacement, motion, pressure, and temperature using advanced transducers.
4 .

To introduce students to advanced biosensor technologies, including non-invasive monitoring systems and biochips, for clinical, industrial, and environmental applications.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Analyze the functional elements and performance characteristics of instrumentation systems and transducers for precise measurements.
2. Demonstrate the ability to select and apply appropriate sensors and transducers for measuring physical and physiological quantities in biomedical and industrial contexts.
3. Design and implement biopotential electrode systems for monitoring ECG, EEG, and EMG signals with minimal interference and artifacts.
4. Evaluate the principles and applications of chemical sensors and biosensors in real-world biomedical, industrial, and environmental scenarios.
5. Integrate advanced biosensor technologies, such as biochips and fiber-optic sensors, into innovative solutions for diagnostics, monitoring, and process control.

Essential Reading

Richard S.C. Cobbold, Transducers for Biomedical Measurements: Principles and Applications, John Wiley & Sons

2 .

Harry N, Norton, Biomedical sensors – fundamentals and application, Harry N, Norton

19196.t: EE6406: Reliability of Power Electronic Converter System
19196.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE6406 : Reliability of Power Electronic Converter System { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module1: Performance factors of power electronic systems. Design objectives for power electronic converters. Reliability requirements in typical power electronic applications. Reliability engineering in power electronics. Physics of failure of power electronic components. DFR of power electronic converter systems. Accelerated testing concepts in reliability engineering. [4 hrs]
Module 2: Anomaly detection and remaining life prediction for power electronics. Failure models. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown models. Energy-based models. Thermal cycling models. FMMEA to identify failure mechanisms. Data-driven methods for life prediction. [7 hrs]
Module 3: Lifetime modelling and prediction of power devices. Failure mechanisms of power modules. Burnout failures. Lifetime metrology: Lifetime and availability, Exponential distribution, Weibull distribution. Redundancy. Lifetime modelling and design of components: Lifetime prediction based on mission profiles, modelling the lifetime of systems with constant failure rate, modelling the lifetime of systems submitted to low-cycle fatigue. Wear-out status of Power modules: On-state voltage measurement method, Current measurement, temperature measurement. Voltage evolution in IGBT/MOSFET and diode: Application of Vce,on monitoring, Degradation and failure mechanisms, Post-mortem investigation. Chip temperature estimation, Processing of state monitoring data. [12 hrs]
Module 4: Reliability of DC-link capacitors in power electronic converters. Failure mechanisms and lifetime models of capacitors. Reliability-oriented design for DC links. Condition monitoring of DC-link capacitors. Capacitor life analysis: Aluminum electrolytic capacitors, Os-con type capacitors. [4 hrs]
Module 5: Active thermal control for improved reliability of power electronics systems. Thermal stress and reliability of power electronics. Concept of active thermal control for improved reliability. Modulation strategies for achieving better thermal loading. Reactive power control achieving better thermal cycling with case studies. Thermal control strategies utilizing active power. Impacts of active power to the thermal stress. Reliability Case studies in different Power Electronics converter system applications like, Renewable Energy System, Electric Vehicle, Power supplies of computers etc. [6 hrs]

Course Objective

1 .

Explain the concept of reliability and its importance in Power electronics Converter system.
2 .

To provide the students a deep insight in to the anomaly detection of power electronics converters and its failure models.
3 .

To expose students for life time modelling, life time prediction of power converter modules along with its components like semiconductor switches, capacitors etc.
4 .

To understand reliability with case studies in various Power Electronics converter dominated system like Renewable Energy System, Electric Vehicle, Power supplies of computers etc

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to
CO1: Understand the basics of reliability and its importance in Power Electronics Converter
System.
CO2: Develop a deep insight in to the anomaly detection power electronics converters and its
failure models.
CO3: Design and develop Life time model and life time prediction model of power converter
modules, Semiconductor switches, capacitors etc
CO4: Develop active thermal control for improved reliability of power electronics systems
CO5: Analyse the reliability in various power conversion system with case studies and its
challenges.

6396.t: PH6114: Non – Linear Dynamics, Chaos and Its Recent Applications
6396.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH6114 : Non – Linear Dynamics, Chaos and Its Recent Applications { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I :Geometrical view of solution of differential equations : vector flow in one and two dimensions. Trajectories in phase space and phase portrait.
Module-II : Linear stability theory . Limit cycle attractor and its existence.
Module-III : Theory and types of bifurcation in one, two and higher dimensions. Poincare map and bifurcation diagram.
Module-IV : Strange attractor in three and higher dimensions and theory of chaotic dynamics. Difference equations and maps. Route to chaos via period doubling. Fractal and fractal dimension. Lyapunov exponent and its numerical methods of calculations
Module-V : Synchronization in coupled systems and network.
Module-VI Introduction to quantum chaos.

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce this new and modern theory of non-linear phenomena, generally not included in traditional course structure and which is mostly unknown to postgraduate students.
2 .

This course particularly useful to address real problems which are in general non-linear and could be studied under approximation by the theories applicable for linear systems.
3 .

It is an interdisciplinary course and so would serve a wider audience.
4 .

This course introduces many complex systems like network in biological systems, electronic circuits.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. The course would facilitate researchers, working in diverse fields of science and engineering and dealing with complex systems, to quantify nature of dynamics arising out of non-linearity.
2. This course would help students to explore interdiscipilinary avenue for further studies.
3. Stusents would learn many numerical techniques which are specifically designed for non-linear differential equations.
4. Students will learn alternative methods of obtaining qualitative results using geometrical methods, than using traditional quantitative result.
5. Students would learn applications of this new theory in diverse fields.
